title: Nail the dreaded Tell me About Yourself Interview Question
description:
Here it comes... the dreaded open-ended "tell me about yourself "question that instantly makes you sweat! In this video, you will learn a simple 4-part strategy to help you crush this question with confidence —no sweat required! I've got you job seekers, and I am going to give you the tools to nail 
it! 

For tips and tricks to write a resume and cover letter that gets interviews, fast, check out my resume and cover letter writing eGuide:

https://katekirchner.thinkific.com/products/digital_downloads/resume-and-cover-letter-writing-guide

For a deeper dive on everything resume and cover letter, that provides step-by-step on- demand instruction, check out my resume writing and cover letter course:

transcript: I think we can all agree that the most cringe-worthy interview question ever is, "Tell me about yourself." Anything but that, right? And most employers open with this. But here's the thing. I've been helping people land jobs for 20 years, and every single one of my clients get asked this question. So today, we're going to break down how to absolutely crush it without feeling stressed. Hey everyone, I'm Kate Kersner. Consider me your career BFF and job search wingwoman. I'll show you how to make your resume, cover letter, and interviews impossible to ignore. I've been doing this for 20 years, but I'm brand new to YouTube. So, I would love for you to join me on my journey, and let's land you that job together. The first piece of information to know how to answer the tell me about yourself question effectively is why the heck are they asking this in the first place? By asking this question, the employer wants to assess three things. who you are, why you love this job, and most importantly, why you're the solution to their problem. Employers also want a genuine connection. Sometimes the person who fits the team and connects actually gets a job over someone with the perfect skills. So, here's my tip. Keep this answer 95% professional. And for the other 5%, let your personality shine. I'm also going to tell you exactly what not to do. Please don't tell your entire life story. Avoid long antidotes like when I was 10, my best friend fell off her bike. I helped her get cleaned up and get a band-aid, which inspired me to be a nurse. But then somewhere in middle school, I realized that blood really freaked me out. So then I decided to be a different kind of helper by going into social work. That passion got ignited when my favorite teacher, Mrs. Miller, took us on a volunteer project. Yikes. That's way too much. you're going to lose your interviewer. And if you're a nervous talker like me, this question can spiral quickly. Or maybe you're the opposite and this question just makes you freeze. I would love to know who gets verbal diarrhea when asked this question, yours truly, and who freezes up. Drop it in the comments. I would love to hear from you. Now, I'm going to give you my four-part strategy to crush it. First, we want to address who we are as a professional. Start with your current role or job title. If it's not a direct match, you're going to want to highlight transferable skills strategically. For example, this is a teacher making the transition from education to HR. I'm a teacher with 10 years of experience building relationships with students and stakeholders. I excel at aligning priorities and fostering collaboration. I worked with diverse quarters and while I love teaching, I'm transitioning into HR. I'm finishing my bachelor's in studying for my sherm certification and I'm excited to apply my relationship building and collaborative skills honed in the education field into the HR field. If your current role aligns with the job, keep it brief, just your job title in one sentence explaining how it's the role that you are a perfect fit for. The second step is outlining what I like to call your career shining moments. What are you most proud of? What is your secret sauce that your bosses and co-workers are always complimenting you on? What are some of the biggest problems you solved? Here is where we want to talk results. Share measurable accomplishments and metrics. Metrics and outcomes are important here because we not only want to address what we did, but we want to let the employer know the impact we have made. This is showing them how we can add value to their team and solve their problems. Add metrics and results that are most relevant to the role you are applying to. You want to start with your most recent role. Here's an example for someone in sales. I took over a struggling territory that had been underperforming. I analyze client outcomes, prioritized high potential leads, and restructured outreach strategies. Within 6 months, I increased revenue by 35%, increased my quota by 20% and onboarded three major accounts that contributed to 40% of the team's total pipeline growth. These results weren't just numbers for me. They transformed our approach and proved that strategy plus perseverance really pays off. I love this because not only does it show measurable results, but it also shows a little bit about the candidates's beliefs that they think results are more than just numbers and they like how persistence pays off. These are good extras for employers to get to know and set you apart. Back to our example of transitioning from the teaching profession to HR. You may want to answer it in this way. I developed a mentorship program that increased student engagement by 25%. My students performance scores increased by more than 10% year-over-year. I engaged parents to get more buyin for their students success and collaborated across departments to align goals and streamline communications, improving outcomes for everyone involved, especially the students. I look forward to bringing my collaborative nature and problem solving skills to the HR field. The third step is talking about why this company, why are you applying for this role addressing this shows that you did your homework. You want to speak to what about this company excites you and why this particular role. If you follow the company on social or use their products, this would be a great time to add this information in as well. Here's an example for someone in sales. I've always admired Salesforce for their focus on customer success and innovation. When I saw their net zero cloud initiative, I was inspired. It aligns with my passion for solutions that create both business and social impact. I want to contribute to meaningful outcomes for clients while driving revenue. This brings us to step four, which is building that connection. This is where I differ from many job coaches. But the reality is, whether fair or not, connection is often more important than knowledge and skills in interviewing situations. So, you need to show the human side of you to make that connection. Here's where you want to give them a tiny glimpse of who you are and share something personal, memorable, and human. Also, keep it appropriate. This is probably not the time to bring up how you received your college nickname. Keep it short, but let your personality shine. Also, think about what personal information can correlate with skills employers are looking for. Here's an example. Keeping us in mind, have completed two marathons. This shows employers you are dedicated and determined. Qualities that will make you a great employee. Now, here's where you can break out your best detective skills. Do some soothing. Glance around the office and see if you notice anything that you could connect on. Is every inch of their office littered with puppy photos? Do they have multiple team posters up? Here are some examples of how to integrate that into your interview. I have a Yorkie poo named Lucy who is basically my sidekick and the best snuggler. Or I'm a huge Milwaukee Brewers fan. If I'm not working, I'm definitely cheering them on. And I noticed a few posters around the office, so I'm guessing you might be a fan, too. Small, genuine touches like that can spark a real connection. The key is don't fake it. Don't pretend to have a pet or a hobby you don't. Authenticity wins every time. Even a single genuine sentence about your life or interest can make the interviewer picture them on the team, and that's often as important as your skills. So interview, here are the four steps to confidently crush this interview question. You want to speak to who you are as a professional, your career, shiny moments with metrics, why this company excites you, and make sure to showcase your personality to make that connection.
